## Day 1 & 2 Flashcards

Press **q** to flip a card, **t** to shuffle and jump to the first card, or use the arrow keys / flip button to navigate.

::: footer
Based on [Day 1 notes](day1.qmd) and [Day 2 notes](day2.qmd).
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Per Joe Cheng's opening quote, what is "winning" the battle between convenience and correctness?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Convenience.

> In the battle between convenience and correctness, convenience is winning.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is "approval fatigue," and why does it undercut the "just add a human reviewer" fix?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
People stop reading agent requests and just click approve — so a human-in-the-loop checkpoint doesn't reliably catch mistakes; the *system* needs to be designed for correctness instead.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What does {commons} do, and what do its three response markers (🟢 🔵 🟡) mean?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
It routes agent questions through **trusted code** the team already relies on instead of always generating bespoke code.

🟢 trusted calculation · 🔵 cited trusted context · 🟡 freehand code (no trust anchor)
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Define **harness**, **tool**, and **agent** per Keyes's talk.
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**harness** — a program that coordinates calls to an LLM and other software systems

**tool** — a function the LLM can ask the harness to run on its behalf

**agent** — an LLM within a harness using tools iteratively in a loop until it accomplishes a task
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
In the patient-chart-summarizer eval, which harness pattern was both the best quality *and* the cheapest — and why?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
The **agent** harness — because it chooses which notes to read via tools instead of re-reading every note every time (unlike the workflow harness).
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
In the NYC Squirrel Count persona study, which persona preserved the most data with the fewest destructive changes, and which discarded the most?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Data manager** — preserved most, fewest destructive changes.

**Environmental researcher** — dropped the most data, made the most assumptions.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are the three "pause, ask, follow directions" skill design rules?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
1. Only pause on decisions that change the question/method/story/interpretation
2. Give just enough context to decide
3. Never editorialize ("great choice," "are you sure?") — present options and follow the user's direction
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What did Brittany (Posit's finance team) build, and what did it save her?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Claude skills to draft finance entries and parse bills, as a non-engineer — saved 5–10 hrs/week, with no sensitive data sent to Anthropic.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What point did the "counting 'n's in unconventional" exercise make?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Asking an LLM directly for a letter count fails, but asking it to *write code* that counts succeeds — because tokens aren't the same thing as letters.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What was Cashorali's closing message, and in what order?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Talk to humans first → agree on what words mean → make sure it's a question worth answering.

> If you don't talk to humans first, AI is a great way to automate misunderstandings.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Give one example of "tribal knowledge" that turned out to need an explicit definition in the pharma project.
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
"Called on" meant *any* interaction (call, email, Zoom, in-office) — not just phone calls. ("Active patient" and "recently" = 30 vs. 60 days were two more.)
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's Sharon Wang's core reframe of "what context do agents need"?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
The durable question is "what context do *you* need" — you can't write down for an agent what you don't understand yourself.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Name two signs it's time to start a new chat instead of pushing through a degraded context window.
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
A new task, a side quest, or catching yourself re-explaining in circles.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's James Wade's reframe of "am I sacrificing capability by staying in R?"
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Agents don't need the largest ecosystem, they need a *coherent* one — only switch languages when there's a compelling reason, not by default.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What does {deputy} add on top of {ellmer}?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Permissions and usage limits on top of ellmer's tool-calling classes — enterprise-style safety controls.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is the "lethal trifecta" (Simon Willison), cited in this talk?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
An agent combining (1) access to private data, (2) exposure to untrusted content, and (3) the ability to communicate out — can be tricked via prompt injection into exfiltrating private data.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
When does a CLI beat a custom MCP server, per Richardson?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
When the CLI already exists, is widely used, and is already in the model's training data (e.g. `gh`) — no context spent teaching the model how to use it.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Why does total conversation cost grow roughly *quadratically*, not linearly, with conversation length?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
LLMs are stateless — every request resends the entire prior conversation, so total spend is the cumulative sum of every growing request.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's the single biggest cost lever Chang highlighted?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Prompt caching — repeated input tokens (in the same order as an earlier request) are served from cache at roughly 1/10th the normal input-token cost.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are Wickham's two "profound but durable" principles for AI-human data science collaboration?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
> Write shit down. And then look at how shit has changed.

(data-dict = write it down; data-diff = look at how it changed)
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What does data-dict record, and how is it shipped?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
A YAML spec of column types/descriptions/examples, table joins, and a glossary of domain terms — shipped as a self-contained Rust CLI (no R/Python runtime needed).
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's the layering of the Shiny AI stack, bottom to top?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
ellmer/chatlas (tidy LLM interface) → shinychat (chat UI toolkit) → domain-specific packages on top, like {commons} and querychat.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is querychat's deliberate capability restriction, and why?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
It restricts agent code execution to SQL/ggsql only — a safety/capability tradeoff that lets read-only DB permissions be enforced at the database layer.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is Positron **Canvas**?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
An early, non-IDE-centric agent surface prototype — collapsed tool calls, a dedicated artifacts pane for plots, and a "live Quarto report mode," built on the same engine as Posit Assistant.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is the **Trajectory reviewer** in Commons?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
It captures real post-deployment user conversations (with disclosure) so the team can see what questions actually came up, then feeds that back into a coding agent to add new measures/context — moving traffic up the trust ladder.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What incident motivated Posit Team's new LLM spend-cap features?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Posit's own team once burned $50,000 unexpectedly running Bedrock-backed deployments on Connect before anyone noticed.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's **destructive-command-guard**, and how does it fix the "agent did something I told it not to" problem?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
An open-source, deterministic pre-tool-call hook that blocks destructive git/package-manager commands before they run — free and fast since it needs no LLM (stronger prompting alone doesn't reliably work).
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Why does the NYT publish a *uniformly* shaded margin-of-error band instead of the more statistically accurate bell-curve band?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
It's a deliberate compromise between statistical correctness and audience familiarity — many readers aren't used to reading a density/histogram shape.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is "non-response bias," and how is it different from sampling error?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Bias from certain kinds of people being less likely to respond to a poll at all — unlike sampling error, it isn't calculable from a simple formula.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is the NYT election-night "needle," and why did the Times *not* use it for the Michigan Senate primary?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Two dials — a margin estimate with an uncertainty band, plus a second dial in words (toss-up / lean X / likely X). Withheld for the primary because polling was so unreliable (off by ~9 points) that the dial's confident-looking swings would have overstated certainty.
:::

## Day 2

::: footer
Cards below are based on [Day 2 notes](day2.qmd).
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Per Wes McKinney's keynote, what three things matter more, not less, in agent-driven work?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Judgment** (deciding what to do), **taste** (knowing when it's good), and **agency** (making it happen) — without them, agent-driven work becomes slop that gets thrown away or left for someone else to maintain.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are the four rules of McKinney's "Clanker Constitution"?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
1. Honor the request
2. Act with judgment — scale process/tooling to the task
3. Verify reality — don't hallucinate results
4. Communicate for humans — plain language, not walls of text
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Per McKinney (via Cory Doctorow), what's the difference between a **centaur** and a **reverse centaur**?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
A centaur is a human assisted by a machine (a "bicycle for the mind"). A reverse centaur is a machine assisted by a human, who just presses the buttons the machine can't press itself — much white-collar AI adoption risks becoming this.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's McKinney's "code isn't actually free" warning?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Generating code feels free, but every line that lands becomes a future burden on every agent session that touches it afterward — "no," and hitting escape, is one of the most powerful tools available.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What accessibility standard does the ADA Title II web rule (and similar legislation) actually point to, per Charlotte Wickham?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
WCAG 2.1 AA (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) — Quarto's job is to translate markdown into accessible markup; the author's job is correct heading structure and alt text.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What was the single biggest category of author-side accessibility violations found on quarto.org?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Missing alt text — 98 violations. Quarto will never generate alt text for you, since only the author knows why a figure is there.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Name two manual accessibility checks that automated tools can't do, per Wickham.
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Tab through with no mouse to confirm you never get stuck; zoom in and confirm text actually gets bigger. (Also: check mobile layout, and review any figures/HTML your own code generates.)
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What is Quarto 2, per Emil Hvitfeldt and Carlos Scheidegger?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
An entirely new, MIT-licensed codebase — a large chunk of Pandoc ported to Rust, compiled to WASM, and run inside the browser. Roughly 100x faster rendering than Quarto 1.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What underlying technology lets Quarto Hub sync edits between collaborators in real time?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Automerge, an open-source CRDT for JSON data — decentralized by design, so collaboration can run fully local or through a hosted service.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What warning did Posit's legal team give about the public Quarto Hub preview?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
"Anything you enter is apparently not protected" — use only for non-sensitive personal experiments; the preview was expected to be turned off again within two weeks.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
How does the NASA Earthdata Cloud Cookbook organize its content, per Andy Teucher?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Explanation (core concepts) → how-to guides (short, task-focused) → tutorials (longer, chaining how-tos) → reference (technical detail/links) — with the contributing guide front-and-center.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are the three pieces of Leslie Emery's clinical data harmonization workflow?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Data model** files (YAML target schema) and **harmonization config** files (YAML mapping per trial) are LLM-drafted; **pipeline code** applies them. Data model + pipeline are one-time setup; configs repeat per data set.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's Mirian Lima's core thesis about "packaging" judgment?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Unpackaged, your judgment dies inside the context window. Packaged (via skills, MCP, hooks, etc.), it accumulates — turning a generic agent into a custom one.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are the four verbs in OSA Metrics' workflow, and what does the last one save?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Discovery → semantic model → iterative Q&A → **save the story, not the answer**: a `session.json` with the table schema and every query/chart pair generated — no raw data, so the analysis is fully reproducible from spec alone.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are Kelli Goggans's three steps for when messy data doesn't fit the question?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Define your limits** (what data you actually need) → **identify standards** (fixed components, validated then followed rigorously) → **refine your analyses** (the question is a North Star, not a strict spec).
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
In Yasha Kaushal's talk, what happened running the same merge prompt on the same 5 files in two different Claude Code sessions?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
407 households one time, 464 the next — with no error thrown. The failure is invisible, there's no decision trail, and a smarter model doesn't fix it since any model still makes its own judgment calls under ambiguity.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's the middle-ground architecture Kaushal's team built instead of "just let Claude Code merge the files"?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
A predetermined schema → **Agent 1** maps raw columns to it (flagging low-confidence mappings for human review) → a **deterministic engine** applies fixed rules → **Agent 2** cross-verifies output and writes a plain-language QA report.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Per Max Kuhn, how do intelligence and wisdom differ for LLMs?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Intelligence is "book smart" (factual, cerebral) — LLMs have plenty. Wisdom is "street smart" (judgment, knowing what *not* to do) — it hasn't caught up, and is hard to teach directly.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's tidymodels' most effective way of building "wisdom" into an API, per Kuhn?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Guardrails baked into the API itself so you can't do feature selection incorrectly through normal use — the final-evaluation function is even named `last_fit()` to signal "this is the last thing you do."
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What selection-bias incident did Kuhn describe almost sinking a real project?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Improper feature-selection validation made a model (~75% of the team's R&D budget) look ~85% accurate. New patient data later showed it was closer to 0% accurate. Lesson: always hold out an unbiased test set, never "double dip."
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's the "real lesson" from Sam Clark's Positron Assistant / DataBot / Posit Assistant story?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Models weren't the bottleneck — they kept improving regardless. The **harness** is what determines whether a model's capabilities take the shape of real data science work.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are Circuit's seven reviewer categories, per Nicky Bell?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Measurement, data-generating process/sampling, causality, sample size & variance/uncertainty, missing data, outliers, and data visualization.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Beyond "good to go," what other verdicts can Circuit return?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Provisional** or **walk away** — designed to say an analysis is unsolvable or fatally flawed rather than always producing an answer.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What are Tyson Barrett's three buckets for any AI task?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Delegate** (trust it fully), **collaborate** (AI types/plans, you decide), **own** (your expertise is essential — full control). Most harnesses default to "delegate," so you have to design your usage deliberately.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Per Barrett, what's the difference in how CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md vs. skills get loaded?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md is read on *every* session, so keep it lean. Skills are triggered only when relevant (via a "use when..." description), so they're cheaper — not loaded into every prompt.
:::

## {background-color="#eef6ff"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What's Jenny Bryan's rule of thumb for excellent file names?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Machine readable, human readable, and self-sorting — her own convention: underscores delimit fields, hyphens delimit words within a field, dates as `YYYY-MM-DD`, left-padded numeric prefixes.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
What problem does Thomas Lin Pedersen's Hephaestus solve for ggplot2, and how?
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
Exported PNGs having the wrong aspect ratio/resolution/colors for a given presentation — solved with a new `.hep` file format: a dynamic, resizable plot object exportable to PNG/JPEG/WebP/SVG/PDF, with live theming.
:::

## {background-color="#fff7e6"}

::: {.flashcard-front}
Define Joe Cheng's three pieces of jargon: bike shedding, onion in the varnish, rubber ducking.
:::

::: {.flashcard-back}
**Bike shedding** — over-debating a trivial detail while high-stakes decisions go unexamined.
**Onion in the varnish** — a step faithfully repeated long after its original reason is gone.
**Rubber ducking** — explaining a problem in detail often reveals the solution yourself.
:::

::: {.flashcard-front}
Nicely done working through Day 1 and Day 2!
